In [[mathematics]], particularly in the field of [[ring theory]], a '''lattice''' is an [[algebraic structure]] which, informally, provides a general framework for taking a sparse set of points in a larger space. Lattices generalize several more specific notions, including [[Lattice (group)|integer lattices]] in [[real number|real]] [[vector space]]s, [[Order (ring theory)|orders]] in [[algebraic number field]]s, and [[fractional ideal]]s in [[integral domains]]. Formally, a lattice is a kind of [[module (mathematics)|module]] over a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] that is [[embedding|embedded]] in a [[vector space]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]].

== Formal definition ==
Let ''R'' be an [[integral domain]] with [[field of fractions]] ''K'', and let ''V'' be a vector space over ''K'' (and thus also an ''R''-module).  An ''R''-[[submodule]] ''M'' of a ''V'' is called a '''lattice''' if ''M'' is [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] over ''R''.  It is called '''full''' if {{nowrap|1=''V'' = ''K'' · ''M''}}, i.e. if ''M'' contains a ''K''-basis of ''V''.<ref>Reiner (2003) pp. 44, 108</ref> Some authors require lattices to be full, but we do not adopt this convention in this article.<ref>Voight (2021) p. 141</ref>

Any finitely-generated [[Torsion-free module|torsion-free]] module ''M'' over ''R'' can be considered as a full ''R''-lattice by taking as the ambient space <math>M \otimes_R K</math>, the [[Change_of_rings#Extension_of_scalars|extension of scalars]] of ''M'' to ''K''. To avoid this ambiguity, lattices are usually studied in the context of a fixed ambient space.

== Properties ==
The behavior of the base ring ''R'' of a lattice ''M'' strongly influences the behavior of ''M''. If ''R'' is a [[Dedekind domain]], ''M'' is completely decomposable (with respect to a suitable basis) as a direct sum of fractional ideals. Every lattice over a Dedekind domain is [[projective module|projective]].<ref>Voight (2021) p. 142</ref>

Lattices are well-behaved under [[Localization (commutative algebra)|localization]] and [[Completion of a ring|completion]]: A lattice ''M'' is equal to the intersection of all the localizations <math>M_{(\mathfrak{p})}</math> of ''M'' at <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>. Further, two lattices are equal if and only if their localizations are equal at all primes. Over a [[Dedekind domain]], the local-global-dictionary is even more robust: any two full ''R''-lattices are equal all but finitely many localizations, and for any choice<ref>We require that the local lattices be ''consistent'', in the sense that there exists some ''R''-lattice ''P'' with <math>P_{(\mathfrak{p})} = N_{(\mathfrak{p})}</math> for all but finitely many primes.</ref> of <math>R_{(\mathfrak{p})}</math>-lattices <math>N_{(\mathfrak{p})}</math> there exists an ''R''-lattice ''M'' satisfying <math>M_{(\mathfrak{p})} = N_{(\mathfrak{p})}</math>. Over Dedekind domains a similar correspondence exists between ''R''-lattices and collections of lattices <math>N_\mathfrak{p}</math> over the completions of ''R'' with respect at primes <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>.<ref>Voight (2021), pp. 143–146</ref>

A pair of lattices ''M'' and ''N'' over ''R'' admit a notion of [[Index of a subgroup|relative index]] analogous to that of integer lattices in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. If ''M'' and ''N'' are projective (e.g. if ''R'' is a Dedekind domain), then ''M'' and ''N'' have trivial relative index if and only if ''M = N''.<ref>Voight 2021, p. 147 f.</ref>

== Pure sublattices ==
An ''R''-submodule ''N'' of ''M'' that is itself a lattice is an ''R''-pure sublattice if ''M''/''N'' is ''R''-torsion-free.  There is a one-to-one correspondence between ''R''-pure sublattices ''N'' of ''M'' and ''K''-[[linear subspace|subspaces]] ''W'' of ''V'', given by<ref>Reiner (2003) p. 45</ref>
: <math>N \mapsto W = K \cdot N ; \quad W \mapsto N = W \cap M. \,</math>
